description: We are a team passionate about technology, science, and creativity. For the NASA Earth Jukebox Challenge, we aim to develop TerraTone, an interactive application that transforms NASA’s Earth visualizations and environmental data into dynamic sound experiences. We want to make Earth science more engaging, inclusive, and accessible. We welcome developers, engineers, sound designers, and creative problem-solvers to help us bring Earth’s story to life through sound.
summary:
We developed TerraTone, an interactive Earth Jukebox that helps people hear and explore our changing planet. It transforms NASA Earth science data into sound generated in real time, synchronized with charts and 3D visualizations. Data values control pitch, loudness, and rhythm, allowing users to listen to environmental patterns while following their visual representations.

TerraTone addresses the challenge’s goal of making Earth science accessible, engaging, and multisensory. Its Earth Jukebox Studio lets users select datasets, explore sound mappings, and save their experiences. Captions, text summaries, keyboard controls, high-contrast settings, and audio-only playback offer different ways to engage with the information. Cached data and simulations also support offline learning.

This matters because complex environmental information can be difficult to understand through images and numbers alone. By combining sound, sight, and interaction, TerraTone offers students, educators, and curious learners another way to recognize patterns and connect with Earth science.
details:
TerraTone is an interactive Earth science application that turns environmental data into sound, synchronized charts, and 3D visualizations. We developed it to help people explore our planet through listening, seeing, and interaction, supporting the Earth Jukebox challenge’s goal of making complex science more accessible and engaging.

How it works

Users select a NASA dataset, a clearly labeled demonstration dataset, or import their own compatible data. TerraTone translates numerical values into musical properties: values influence pitch, magnitude influences loudness within controlled limits, and geographic longitude can influence stereo position. As the data plays, a moving chart indicator, captions, and a 3D data landscape follow the same timeline.

The Earth Jukebox Studio allows users to explore sound mappings, preview their choices, and save or export experiences. Different sound profiles offer musical, ambient, minimal, and scientific listening styles.

TerraTone integrates NASA POWER environmental data, EONET natural-event records, and EPIC and APOD imagery. It also includes interactive 3D simulations with synthesized environmental sounds. Simulations and demonstration datasets are labeled separately from NASA observations. Optional AI explanations provide another way to explore the material and are identified as AI-generated.

Benefits and intended impact

TerraTone gives learners another way to recognize changes and patterns that may be difficult to understand through numbers or visualizations alone. Captions, text summaries, audio-only playback, keyboard controls, high-contrast settings, adjustable text sizes, and reduced-motion options support different needs and preferences.

Offline access to cached datasets and simulations helps users continue learning where internet connectivity is limited. Our intended impact is to support more inclusive Earth science education, encourage curiosity about environmental change, and help students, teachers, and the public connect with NASA data.

Tools and technologies

We built TerraTone using TypeScript, JavaScript, React, HTML, and CSS, with Vite for development and production builds. The Web Audio API generates sonifications and procedural sound effects, while Three.js creates interactive 3D environments and data visualizations. Leaflet supports geographic event maps.

Service workers and IndexedDB provide offline caching and local storage. Electron supports the Windows desktop version, and Capacitor supports Android packaging. Vitest supports automated testing. Optional explanations use Google Gemini, while browser speech synthesis reads text aloud. Users can access the project through a compatible computer or smartphone, with speakers or headphones for listening. No specialized hardware is required.

Creativity and design considerations

TerraTone combines a data instrument with an interactive learning environment. Users can hear environmental patterns, watch those patterns take shape, and explore simulated environments whose sounds respond to their actions.

Our team considered accessibility, understandable sound mappings, controlled audio levels, device performance, limited connectivity, and clear data attribution. We distinguish measured data from synthetic examples, simulations, and AI explanations so users understand what they are experiencing. Sound serves as a companion to scientific information.

The current implementation synchronizes NASA datasets with TerraTone’s own visualizations. Direct pairing with Earth Information Center visual frames remains a next development step toward meeting the challenge’s full specification.
